A new release needs only this file updated and the screenshots re-captured (node tools/guide/shots.mjs), then node tools/guide/build.mjs and node tools/guide/verify.mjs. Inline markup in text: **ui label** (bold), [[Key]] (a keyboard key), _emphasis_, {play} {prev} {next} {back12} {fwd12} (icons of the transport buttons). A figure's callouts point at elements named in the shot's `elements` map; the boxes are measured on the live build when the shot is captured.

chapters.title: Start here
chapters.sub: Opening the map, your first visit, the screen at a glance
chapters.lead: The map replays the Battle of Gettysburg, July 1–3, 1863, as 675 moments. Press play and watch the two armies move, or stop on any moment and look closely.

blocks.text: Open [gettysburginteractivemap.com](https://gettysburginteractivemap.com/) in a current browser. There is nothing to install and no account to create. Phones and touch tablets up to 834 pixels wide get the phone layout (chapter 9); everything else gets the desktop layout, described first.
A welcome window asks how you want to explore. It does not appear again once you have skipped it or finished a path.

blocks.caption: The welcome window. **Skip introduction** closes it.

head: Choice
What happens
rows: A five-step introduction: Dawn on July 1, First Artillery Fire, Reynolds Killed, The Crisis at Little Round Top and Pickett’s Charge. Each step explains what you are looking at and suggests one thing to do. **Skip tour** leaves it at any point.
Goes straight to the map at July 1.
Shows the Quick Reference: [[Space]], the arrow keys, [[1]] [[2]] [[3]], [[+]] [[-]], [[S]], [[F]] and [[?]]. **Start exploring** closes it.

chapters.title: Moving through time
chapters.lead: Everything on the map belongs to a moment. The timeline along the bottom of the screen chooses which one, and plays the battle forward from there.

blocks.caption: The timeline on July 1 at about 11:20 PM.

callouts.title: Clock
callouts.text: The date and time of the moment you are looking at.

callouts.title: Day buttons
callouts.text: **July 1**, **July 2** and **July 3** jump to the first moment of that day. The current day is highlighted.

callouts.title: Event markers
callouts.text: Coloured dots along the bar mark key events in the battle.

callouts.title: Scrubber
callouts.text: Drag the handle, or click the bar, to go to any moment from July 1 to July 3.

callouts.title: Playback buttons
callouts.text: {back12} back one hour · {prev} back one step · {play} play or pause · {next} forward one step · {fwd12} forward one hour.

callouts.title: Speed
callouts.text: Six speeds from **1/4x** to **8x**. The one in use is highlighted.

callouts.title: Time of day
callouts.text: The same time again, in words, beside the speed buttons. The screen shows times of day; the numbers 1 to 675 that number the moments appear only in links (chapter 6).

items: Press {play} **Play**, or press [[Space]]. Units begin to move and the clock runs.
Press it again to pause.
Drag the scrubber, or click anywhere on the bar, to move to another moment. The map updates as you go.
Click **July 2** or **July 3**, or press [[2]] or [[3]], to jump to the start of that day. [[1]] returns to the start of July 1.

blocks.text: The {prev} and {next} buttons move one step at a time, to the next moment of the battle. {back12} and {fwd12} move about an hour of battle time. Steps are not all the same length: a step can be a few minutes or much more, so read the clock, not the number of steps.

Click a speed button, or use the keys: [[+]] doubles the speed, [[-]] halves it and [[0]] returns to **1x**. The keys reach 16 times speed and one quarter speed; the buttons cover 1/4x to 8x. The label at the top left of the map names the speed, for example **1x (base speed)** or **8x (fast)**.

rows: Forward about one hour of battle time.
Jump to the July 1 tab, about 5:00 AM.
Jump to the July 2 tab, about 4:30 AM.
Jump to the July 3 tab, about 4:15 AM.

blocks.title: About the clock
blocks.text: Times are approximate. Sources disagree by half an hour or more, and the map plays as a time-lapse.

chapters.title: Reading the map
chapters.sub: Moving the map, units, the legend, cards
chapters.lead: Each regiment, battery and larger formation on the field is a flag on a map of the ground as it was in July 1863. The colour of a flag tells you the side and its shape the arm; a click tells you everything else.

head: To
Do this
rows: Press on the map and drag.
Scroll the wheel over the map, or use the **+** and **–** buttons at the top right. The compass button under them turns the map back to face north.
Press [[Tab]] until the map has focus. The arrow keys then pan the map, [[+]] and [[-]] zoom it, and [[Shift]] with the arrow keys rotates and tilts it. [[Esc]] hands the keys back to the clock.

blocks.text: The map is a reconstruction of July 1863, not a photograph of it: a 2013 aerial photograph of the field with later features removed and 1863 features added from period maps. A box at the top of the map says so in every view. **Show what was changed** colours the parts that were removed, filled, drawn or recoloured, with a key, and **Sources and licences** opens the credits. The box moves out of the way when a card needs the room.

A unit is a flag on a pole; the foot of the pole is the unit’s place on the ground. Blue is Union and red is Confederate. The shape says the arm: a square-ended flag is infantry, a swallow-tailed flag is cavalry and an arrow-ended flag is artillery. A flag flies toward the enemy, the Union’s to the right and the Confederate’s to the left. A label names the unit, such as **1st Minnesota**, or the formation, such as **Early’s Div, 2nd Corps**. Where several units stand close together they are drawn as one larger flag with a number in it: the number of placement records it stands for, never a count of men. Zoom in, or click it, and it splits. The flags move as the clock runs. A unit that is not on the field at that moment is not drawn.

The legend at the left of the map is called **What the marks say**. Every row says what a mark means and carries a label for how well that is known: **Documented** (printed in the order of battle), **Modelled** (placed by hand, not recorded), **Computed** (counted by a stated rule), **Contested** (the records disagree) or **Design** (drawn to be read). A mark with no record behind it says so in its own label. **More marks** opens the rest of the rows and **How the marks are drawn** opens a picture of one flag taken apart.

items.caption: The rest of the rows: how old a position is, crowds, strength, the selected mark.

blocks.caption: Marks and what they claim
head: Mark
Meaning
rows: Union, from the order of battle.
Confederate, from the order of battle.
The side is not known. The flag is hatched and never takes a side colour.
A crowd of both sides in one mark.
A formation record (brigade, division or corps). No arm is claimed.
The latest position on record is under half a battle day old.
The position is a battle day or more old and is carried forward.
The placement records it stands for, never men.
No order-of-battle record: the name comes from the unit’s id alone.
The selected mark. From zoom 15 it also shows its name.
A bar under a regiment flag
The strength in the placement record against a reference strength. A bar at 40 % is a recorded value, not a count of casualties.

blocks.text: Click a unit to open its card at the left of the screen. The card follows the clock: its details change as the unit’s situation changes. Press [[Esc]] or the close button to dismiss it.
Rest the pointer on a flag and a small card names the unit and its formation, with the same evidence labels as the legend.

blocks.text: At key moments the map shows cards. A **story card** tells one episode in a few paragraphs. An **event card** gives a one-line rating, the time and a summary.

blocks.caption: July 2 at about 7:05 PM shows both kinds of card.

callouts.title: Story card
callouts.text: The title, how long it takes to read, and the unit it is about.

callouts.title: Jump button
callouts.text: Shows the time of the story’s moment. Click it to move the clock there.

callouts.title: Dismiss
callouts.text: Closes the story card.

callouts.title: Event card
callouts.text: A rating such as **CRITICAL**, the time, and what happened. It has its own close button.

blocks.text: Trails, the overview and hiding units

items: **Trails ON** and **Trails OFF**, at the top right of the map, switch unit trails on and off.

**Overview** is the small map at the bottom right. It shows every unit on the field, and its caption counts them, for example **192 units · about 11:20 PM**. Close it with its close button or press [[M]].

**Toggle Units** in the top bar hides every unit at once so you can read the ground; press it again to bring them back. The clock and all other tools keep working. On a narrow window or a phone it moves into **More to Explore** or **Tools**.

chapters.title: The toolbar
chapters.lead: Thirteen buttons at the top right of the screen open the tools of the map. Five of them also answer to a key.

blocks.caption: The toolbar, left to right. The numbers match the table below.

rows.name: Search
rows.text: Find a unit by name, state, commander or id.

rows.name: Filter
rows.text: Show only some sides, unit types, dispositions or strengths.

rows.name: Unit Roster
rows.text: List every unit with its commander and status.

rows.name: Legend
rows.text: Show or hide the legend, What the marks say.

rows.name: Monuments
rows.text: Draws the 512 battlefield monuments and the 20 story stars on the map. Click one for its card. **Browse monuments** lists them for the keyboard. Press the button again to hide them.

rows.name: Soldier’s Eye View (Street View)
rows.text: Eight viewpoints that open in Google Street View.

rows.name: Follow Your Ancestor
rows.text: Follow one regiment through all three days.

rows.name: Distance Tool
rows.text: Measure the distance between two points on the map.

rows.name: Map Layers
rows.text: Turn the road and river lines and their names, the breastworks and the farm names on and off.

rows.name: Locations
rows.text: Show or hide the place-name labels.

rows.name: Find Unit / Location
rows.text: Opens the same search panel as **Search**.

rows.name: Bookmarks
rows.text: Copy a link to this moment, or save it.

rows.name: Help
rows.text: Keyboard shortcuts and a short About.

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.text: A highlighted button means its tool is on. **Legend** and **Locations** start highlighted.

callouts.title: Search box
callouts.text: Type a unit name, a state, a commander or a unit id.

callouts.title: Sort
callouts.text: **relevance** puts the best match first; **casualties** sorts them by casualty percentage.

after.text: Press [[S]] or click **Search**. Before you type, the panel lists a few notable units: the 20th Maine, 1st Minnesota, Iron Brigade, 26th NC, Cushing’s Battery, Armistead and 15th Alabama. Choose a result and the map moves to that unit and its card opens.
**Find Unit / Location** opens this same panel.

callouts.title: Side
callouts.text: Turn Union or Confederate off and on.

callouts.title: Unit type
callouts.text: Infantry, Cavalry or Artillery.

callouts.title: Disposition
callouts.text: Eleven states of what a unit is doing, such as Line of Battle or Bivouac.

callouts.title: Minimum strength
callouts.text: A slider from **All** through 100 and 250 to 500+.

callouts.title: Close
callouts.text: Closes the panel. Filters stay in force.

after.text: Press [[F]] or click **Filter**. A badge beside the title, such as **1 active**, counts the filters in force, and **Reset** puts everything back. Filtering changes what the map draws; it does not change the clock.

blocks.caption: The roster on July 2 at about 7:05 PM.

callouts.title: Union column
callouts.text: Every Union unit in the order of battle, with its count.

callouts.title: Confederate column
callouts.text: Every Confederate unit, with its count.

callouts.title: Close
callouts.text: Closes the roster.

after.text: Each row gives a unit’s name and commander. Units on the field at this moment show their status; the others read **Not on field**. The lists scroll separately.

A list of eight places on the field: Little Round Top, The Angle, McPherson’s Ridge, Devil’s Den, the Wheatfield, Cemetery Hill, Culp’s Hill and the Peach Orchard. Each entry opens that spot in Google Street View, so you can stand where the soldiers stood. The viewer is provided by Google.

blocks.caption: The 20th Maine, followed through the battle.

items: Click **Follow Your Ancestor**.
Type a regiment name, such as 20th Maine, and choose it from the list.
The panel names the regiment and lists **every recorded position for this regiment, in order**, with the day, time and what happened. The unit card opens.
**Copy link** copies a link that opens the map on this regiment. **Change Regiment** goes back to the list.

after.text: The site lists regiments, not individual soldiers. To find a soldier by name, search the National Park Service’s Soldiers and Sailors System.

items: Click **Distance Tool**. The panel reads **Click map for point A**.
Click the map for point A, then for point B.
The panel shows the distance in feet, yards and metres, and an estimated march time in minutes.
Click the map again to start a new measurement.

after.text: Each check box turns one layer on or off: **1863 Roads**, **Road Labels**, **Rivers**, **River Labels**, **Breastworks** and **Farm Labels**. **Road Labels**, **River Labels** and **Breastworks** start on; the roads, rivers and farms are already part of the reconstructed ground.
**Locations** is a single button. It shows or hides the place names such as Seminary Ridge, Cemetery Hill and Culp’s Hill.

Press [[B]] or click **Bookmarks**. **Copy Link** copies a link to the moment on screen. **+ Bookmark current moment** asks for a name, with the moment already filled in, and **Save** adds it to the list of saved bookmarks. See chapter 6 for what a link remembers.

blocks.text: Press [[?]] or click **Help**. The **Keyboard Shortcuts** tab lists every key (chapter 8). The **About** tab names the sources behind the map. [[Tab]] stays inside the dialog while it is open, and [[Esc]] closes it.

chapters.title: Virtual Walkthrough and Tour
chapters.lead: Two ways to see the ground as it is today: a tour of sixteen stops with narration and Street View, and a searchable list of every monument.

blocks.text: Click **Virtual Walkthrough** in the top bar. The screen changes to a map at the left and a reading panel at the right. **Back to the map** returns you to the battle.

blocks.caption: The Virtual Walkthrough at Tour Stop 1, McPherson Ridge.

callouts.title: Back to the map
callouts.text: Returns to the battle map.

callouts.title: Map layers
callouts.text: Two check boxes show or hide the numbered tour stops and the monuments.

callouts.title: Tabs
callouts.text: **Tour Stops** and **Monuments**.

callouts.title: Stop buttons
callouts.text: Sixteen numbered buttons, one per stop. The map and the narration follow your choice.

callouts.title: Narration
callouts.text: The story of the stop, then a Google Street View panorama, an **Open in Google Maps** link and an NPS video link.

callouts.text: Type part of a monument’s name or unit.

callouts.title: Side

callouts.title: Group

after.text: The list shows the first 100 matches at a time. Each entry gives the monument’s name, its number, who it honours, where it stands, its latitude and longitude and a **View on map** link.

blocks.text: The **NPS Auto Tour** button at the bottom right of the battle map starts the same sixteen stops over the live map. The map moves to each stop and the clock moves to the stop’s moment. Press [[Esc]] to leave the tour.

chapters.title: Share and return
chapters.lead: Every view of the map can be put in a link. Send it to someone and they open the same moment, the same unit and the same view.

items: **Bookmarks** ([[B]]): **Copy Link** copies a link to the moment on screen.
The unit card: its first button copies a link that selects that unit.
**Follow Your Ancestor**: **Copy link** opens the map on that regiment.
**Documentary Mode** links each story to its exact moment on the map (chapter 7).
Move to the moment you want to keep.
Press [[B]] and click **+ Bookmark current moment**.
Edit the name if you like, and click **Save**. The bookmark appears under **Saved Bookmarks**. **Cancel** discards it.

blocks.text: A link is the address of the map followed by a question mark and one or more settings joined with &. The map reads them when it opens. A setting it cannot use is ignored, and the map opens in its usual place instead.

blocks.caption: Link settings
head: Setting
Meaning
rows: A moment from 1 to 675. If you give both `tick` and `day`, `tick` wins.
1, 2 or 3: the first moment of that day.
A unit id such as U-1MN. The unit is selected and its card is pinned.
A story id. The map moves to the moment of that story. Used only when there is no valid `tick` or `day`.
A regiment id. Opens Follow Your Ancestor on that regiment.
Map centre as latitude,longitude, for example `39.8112,-77.2260`. Accepted only inside the battlefield. `lat` and `lng` work in place of `ll`.
`mobile` or `desktop`: forces the phone or the desktop layout.

chapters.title: The other pages
chapters.sub: Ask the Historian and the More to Explore menu
chapters.lead: Beyond the map, the site has nineteen pages for searching, reading, researching and sharing. They all open from two buttons at the left of the map, under the day and the time.

callouts.title: More to Explore

callouts.title: Hide button

before.text: Click **More to Explore**. The menu groups the pages by what you want to do. Click a page to open it in the same window; every page has a **Back to the map** link.

blocks.text: At the foot of each page are links to **Privacy**, **Terms**, **Contact** and **User Guide (PDF)**.

blocks.title: Battlefield AR
blocks.text: A page for use on the field, with a phone that has a camera, GPS and compass. It is in beta and is not listed in the menu; it opens at gettysburginteractivemap.com/ar.html. Compass accuracy varies by phone, so treat its markers as a guide to direction, not a survey.

items.title: Search Everything
items.text: Type a regiment, a story or a place. The tabs **All**, **Regiments**, **Vignettes** and **Locations** narrow the results.

items.title: Compare Moments
items.text: Two maps side by side, each with its own slider and its own style: **Satellite**, **Dark**, **Parchment** or **3D Terrain**. Compare the Union line at 4:00 PM with the same line at 6:00 PM.

items.title: Camera Modes
items.text: **Director Mode** flies the camera to wherever the most units are engaged. **Follow a Unit** locks onto one regiment and tracks it through the battle.

items.title: High Ground
items.text: Pick one of thirty places from the list, from Big Round Top (785 ft) down, and see its height. It ranks elevation only; trees, buildings and smoke often decided what a soldier could see.

items.title: What-If Sandbox
items.text: Pick a starting moment, load it, then drag units and change their status. It is hypothetical and not history. Nothing is saved, and reloading resets it.

items.title: Ask the Historian
items.text: Type a question about a regiment, a commander, a place or a moment, or choose a suggestion such as 20th Maine or Pickett’s Charge, then press **Ask**. Answers come only from this site’s own records.

items.title: Documentary Mode
items.text: All 24 key moments of the battle in order, each with its full account and a link to its place on the map. **Previous** and **Next** move between them.

items.title: Turning Points
items.text: Nine numbered decisions where the battle could have gone differently. Click one to open what happened and how historians have argued it.

items.title: For Students
items.text: A short guide to the battle in three tabs, **Day 1: July 1**, **Day 2: July 2** and **Day 3: July 3**, told through the people who were there.

items.title: Aftermath
items.text: What happened to the two armies, the town and the ground from July 4 to November 1863. It is an overview, not built from the unit-by-unit records of the map.

items.title: Regimental Biography
items.text: Search for a regiment or battery and read its three days as one story.

items.title: Find Your Ancestor
items.text: Choose a state, or type a commander’s surname, to narrow down the regiments an ancestor may have served in. It lists regiments, not individual soldiers.

items.title: Casualty Dashboard
items.text: Corps-by-corps strength across the three days. Switch Union or Confederate corps on and off, or click a legend entry to isolate one corps. The curves are modelled from each corps’ recorded engagement periods.

items.title: Regiment Fact Sheets
items.text: Search for a regiment and make a one-page fact sheet. Print it, or save it as a PDF with your browser’s print dialog.

items.title: Immersive Mode
items.text: A soundscape made in your browser that follows how many units are engaged at each moment. You turn the sound on yourself with **Enable Sound & Start**, and set the **Volume**.

items.title: The Living Ledger
items.text: A running total of casualties, split into Union and Confederate, climbing across the three days. **Play**, **Restart**, and choose 1x, 3x or 10x.

items.title: The Ground Remembers
items.text: Every recorded unit position, accumulated on one map, so the places where units stood most often stand out. **Build up over time** replays it; the slider reveals it through any moment.

items.title: Watch Together
items.text: Build a guided tour with your own stops and notes and share it as a file with **Export tour**. **Start a live session** shares a five-letter code so a second browser follows along; it can be unavailable, and exporting always works.

items.title: Export a Video
items.text: Choose a start and end moment, a length of 8, 15 or 30 seconds and caption settings, then **Record** a video of the camera flying across that stretch. It is made in your browser and nothing is uploaded.

Move focus to the map. Then the arrow keys pan, [[Plus]] and [[Minus]] zoom, and [[Shift]] with the arrow keys rotates and tilts.

blocks.text: Using the map from the keyboard

items: The first two links on the page, **Skip to the map** and **Skip to the timeline controls**, appear when you press [[Tab]]. Use them to jump past the toolbar.
Keep pressing [[Tab]] to move through the buttons. [[Enter]] or [[Space]] presses the focused button.
Press [[S]] to search. Type a name, press [[Down]] to move into the results and [[Enter]] to choose one.
Press [[Tab]] until the map has focus to pan and zoom with the keys. Press [[Esc]] to return the arrow keys to the clock.
The scrubber is a slider named **Battle time**; it announces the moment as a date and time, for example July 1, 6:00 AM.
Playback buttons are named in full: **Play**, **Previous step**, **Next step**, **Back one hour** and **Forward one hour**. The toolbar buttons are named too.
The search panel announces how many results there are and how to reach them.
The unit card is a region named **Unit details**. Panels and dialogs have names, and the Help dialog keeps focus inside it until you close it.

blocks.title: Press ? for the list
blocks.text: The Help dialog lists the keys with the version of the map you are using, so it is always the most current reference.

chapters.title: Good to know
chapters.sub: What the map does and does not claim
chapters.lead: A few notes on how to read the map, and on places where this release differs from what its labels suggest.

items: Positions are reconstructed from published sources. Where a regiment’s exact place at a given time is not recorded, the map shows the best-supported position.
Times are approximate. Sources disagree by half an hour or more, and the map plays as a time-lapse.
Casualties are men killed, wounded, and captured or missing, added together.
The site lists regiments, not individual soldiers. To find a soldier by name, search the National Park Service’s Soldiers and Sailors System.
The clock gives times of day: **about 11:20 PM**. Each time carries a tolerance, for example give or take 25 minutes; rest the pointer on the clock to read it. The date is always July 1, 2 or 3.
Steps are not equal in length, and **one hour** on the Help panel means about an hour of battle time on the clock. Read a step as a place in the story, not a fixed length of time.
A mark never claims more than its label says: **Documented**, **Modelled**, **Computed**, **Contested** or **Design**.
The heatmap key and the in-map sound switch of earlier versions are gone. **The Ground Remembers** shows where fighting concentrated, and **Immersive Mode** plays sound.

The ground is a reconstruction of July 1863, not a photograph: a 2013 aerial photograph with later features removed and 1863 features drawn in from period maps. **Show what was changed** shows where it was altered.

end.title: Questions and corrections
paras: Found something wrong, or something missing? Write to [gettysburginteractivemap@gmail.com](mailto:gettysburginteractivemap@gmail.com) and say which page and which moment you were on.
